newsitem.title: NORWAY: Nobel winner says Jakarta breaks diplomatic rules.
newsitem.headline: Nobel winner says Jakarta breaks diplomatic rules.

text.p: Nobel Peace Prize co-winner Jose Ramos Horta accused Jakarta on Wednesday of putting pressure on fellow laureate Carlos Belo of East Timor not to use this week's awards ceremony in Oslo to attack Indonesia.

"It shows the nature of the Indonesian regime that even in a country as peaceful, open and democratic as Norway it interferes, it abuses diplomatic privileges," Ramos Horta told Norwegian NRK television.

He was referring to Norwegian news reports that the Indonesian embassy had put pressure on the often outspoken Roman Catholic bishop, who shared the peace prize on Tuesday with the self-exiled independence campaigner.
"The Indonesian embassy is in breach (of) diplomatic practice and this is an offence, I believe, against Norway," Ramos Horta said.

Indonesian ambassador Aminruddin Noor has dismissed suggestions that attempts to pressure Belo had been made. The two men were honoured for their efforts to achieve a peaceful solution to the conflict in East Timor, which was invaded by Indonesia in December 1975 and annexed seven months later. The move is not recognised by the United Nations which regards old colonial master Portugal as the administering power.

Norwegian Foreign Minister Bjoern Tore Godal, after seeing Ramos Horta and Belo earlier in the day, sought to play down the accusations that Indonesia had sought to influence the bishop's activities in Oslo.
"He did not seem particularly under pressure," Godal said.
Nobel Committee Chairman Francis Sejersted, asked the same question, said: "I don't know. The Indonesian government has obviously been very active in many ways."
Belo, stressing he is a religious leader, has dodged political questions in meetings with reporters in the Norwegian capital. In his Nobel speech, he called for reconciliation.
Indonesia, which boycotted the award ceremony, has condemned the Norwegian Nobel Committee's decision to include Ramos Horta in the prestigious prize.

In his Nobel speech, the veteran resistance leader presented proposals for gradual East Timor self-determination, sharply criticised the Indonesian stance but called on Jakarta to enter a dialogue on a peace settlement.
He said after seeing Godal he believed Jakarta would one day listen to his proposals for peace in the Indonesia-ruled territory.

"In the long run they will come around and talk with us, like South Africa in the end had to talk with Mandela," he said in a reference to South African President Nelson Mandela, a 1993 Nobel Peace Prize co-winner.
